concept.title: How Content Fusion Finds DITA References
concept.shortdesc: The References tab of the Explore side view shows how the files of a DITA project reference each other. Use it to find what a change affects before you make it, and to learn how a large project fits together.

conbody.note: The References tab is experimental. To turn it on, open your Profile page and, in the Preferences section, select Show the DITA References tab in the Explore side view. The setting applies to the current browser only. The tab is available in projects that define publications.

section.title: Where the References Come From
section.p: The tab reads the files of your workspace in the browser. It starts from the root map of each publication and follows every reference it finds, so it reaches every file that a publication uses. A file that no publication reaches has no references in the tab.
The tab finds these kinds of references:

strow.stentry: topicref, mapref, keydef, key definitions, aliases made with copy-to, reltable, ditavalref, subject scheme references, and the publications of the project file
conref, conkeyref, conref push, coderef, and include
image, media, object, and other references to files that are not DITA

p.note: DITA specializations that use different element names are not currently supported.

section.p: The tab joins the files of the project into a graph. Each file, key or URL that it finds is a node, and each reference links two nodes. The tab shows the nodes as a tree, one level for each step along the references. The kind of a node is one of: map, topic, key, alias, resource (an image or another file that is not DITA), URL, DITAVAL, missing file, or unreadable file.

section.title: Incoming references
section.p: The nodes that the current file references are easy to compute by just inspecting the current file. The References tab also shows where a file is referenced in the Referenced by tab. After the tab loads, you can navigate incoming references of any file instantly.

section.title: Project Scope and Publication Scope
section.p: By default, the tab covers the whole project: every file that any publication uses. In this project scope:

ul.li: The tab applies no profiling, so it shows every reference, even if its excluded in all the publications.
The tab does not resolve keys by key scope. All the keys with the same name are one node even when they belong to different key scopes.

section.p: The Use the context publication as scope toolbar button limits the tab to the context publication. In this publication scope, the tab processes the maps as the publication does: it applies the DITAVAL profiling, resolves keys in their key scopes, and follows copy-to. A file that the publication leaves out has no references in this scope.
Use the project scope to find everything that a change can affect, in every publication. Use the publication scope to see what one publication includes, or why a key resolves the way it does.

section.title: When the Tab Reads the Files
section.p: The tab reads the files when it opens and keeps what it found. It does not follow your edits, saves or commits. After you change files, click Refresh to read them again.
Reading a large project takes a while, and the tab shows its progress. While it reads, more references to the shown file can still appear in the Referenced by list.

ul.li: The tab treats XML files that are not DITA, and files in formats that it does not know, as resources. It does not look for references inside them.
In the publication scope, the tab does not apply chunking, and it ignores the linking attribute.
Large projects take longer to read.
